content:
A JavaScript website can work perfectly after a visitor clicks through from its homepage and still fail when someone opens an article URL directly. Technical SEO starts by following that direct request: what the server returns, what the browser adds, and which content remains available when a dependency fails. This guide is a diagnostic workflow for public articles, documentation, and product pages. It does not promise indexing or rankings.

Define a small set of representative routes

Choose one article, one category, one paginated listing, one redirected URL, and one nonexistent path. Include a route that loads content from an API. Write down each expected status, title, main heading, canonical URL, and primary internal links. This route sheet becomes your acceptance checklist; a successful homepage check cannot stand in for the other templates.

Use an ordinary logged-out browser profile. Record whether consent, location, or stored settings change the public content. Keep private account pages outside this exercise. The goal is to make the same intended public information available through direct navigation, internal links, and the rendered page.

Inspect the response before examining the interface

In a terminal with curl available, replace the example address with a route you control. These commands inspect responses without changing the website. On Windows, use curl.exe where curl is a shell alias.

curl -I https://example.com/guides/javascript-seo
curl -sS -D - https://example.com/guides/javascript-seo
curl -sS -L -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code} %{url_effective}
' https://example.com/old-guide

The first command sends HEAD; the second sends GET and includes response headers. If HEAD is unsupported or behaves differently, use GET as the evidence for the page response. The third follows redirects and reports the final address and status on a POSIX shell; replace /dev/null with NUL on Windows. Inspect intermediate redirects separately when diagnosing loops or unnecessary hops.

A public page should return the status appropriate to its actual state. A missing article that displays an error inside a successful app shell needs attention. Test a deliberately nonexistent route and a deleted content identifier. Write down whether the server distinguishes those cases from an existing article. Do not solve this by hiding all routes from search.

Compare initial HTML and rendered content

Save or inspect the GET response, then inspect the browser document after scripts complete. Look for the article text, meaningful headings, links, title, and canonical in both versions. An empty initial article container is a dependency worth documenting, even when the browser eventually fills it. In developer tools, check failed requests and console errors while loading the route directly.

Google describes crawling, rendering, and indexing as separate stages in its JavaScript SEO documentation. That distinction helps explain why seeing content in your own browser is insufficient evidence about a search engine's processed page. Google's JavaScript troubleshooting guide provides the corresponding inspection methods. A logged-out local check and a Search Console inspection answer different questions.

Choose rendering according to the content

For an evergreen article, static generation can deliver complete HTML with straightforward hosting and caching. Its tradeoff is a publishing pipeline that must rebuild or invalidate stale pages. Server rendering suits frequently changing public data but adds request-time work and failure modes. Client rendering can remain appropriate for interactive controls and private dashboards. A hybrid page can send the article first and enhance filters or bookmarks afterward.

Choose the smallest change that removes the observed dependency. Replacing an entire framework is rarely a useful first diagnostic step. If you introduce server rendering, compare the server output and hydrated document for mismatched titles, duplicated content, and stale article data. A rendering change also needs operational ownership.

Make routes discoverable through real links

A visitor should be able to reach the article from a relevant category or related guide through a normal link. For example, use <a href="/guides/javascript-seo">JavaScript SEO checklist</a>. A clickable container with only an event handler leaves link behavior dependent on code and can remove familiar actions such as opening a new tab.

Follow Google's crawlable-link guidance when inspecting navigation. Review pagination as well as individual cards. A listing that only reveals more articles after a button press deserves a separate discovery check. Descriptive anchor text should explain the destination; repeating a keyword in every link makes navigation less useful.

Keep identity and metadata consistent

For each route, compare the visible article title with its document title and description. They need not be identical, but they should describe the same page. Navigate between two articles without reloading, then refresh each directly. This exposes metadata that updates on one navigation path but remains stale on another.

Choose a preferred address for genuinely equivalent URL variants. Check that internal links, sitemap entries, redirects, and canonical markup support that choice. Google's canonicalization guidance explains that canonical annotations are signals, rather than a guaranteed selection. Canonicalizing unrelated articles to one destination does not repair weak editorial content.

Test failure states and document release evidence

On a staging environment, block the article API or simulate its failure with browser request blocking. Check whether the page shows an understandable error, exposes stale information as current, or spins indefinitely. Then test a slow connection and direct navigation to a nested path. These checks reveal dependencies; they are not measurements of real visitor performance.

  • Record the URL, date, response status, and final redirect destination.
  • Confirm the intended text and heading appear after rendering.
  • Verify article links and pagination without relying on stored session state.
  • Compare canonical and metadata before and after client navigation.
  • Retest the missing route and failed API response.
  • If authorized Search Console access exists, inspect representative URLs and retain the observed result.

Assign each failure to its template or dependency so one fix can be checked across affected routes. Keep an unresolved item open when evidence is unavailable. The useful deliverable is a reproducible route checklist with specific findings, not a declaration that the whole website is SEO complete. Search visibility also depends on content usefulness and other factors beyond these technical checks.
excerpt: Diagnose JavaScript SEO route by route: inspect HTTP responses, compare rendered content, verify links and canonicals, and record failure-state evidence.
seoTitle: Technical SEO for a JavaScript Website
seoDescription: A practical JavaScript SEO workflow for HTTP responses, rendering, links, metadata, canonicals, and failure states, with commands and a release checklist.

content:
AI-generated code deserves the same accountable review as any other proposed change. The difficulty is that a polished explanation can make unfamiliar code feel understood before anyone has checked its behavior. A useful human workflow separates the intended contract, the actual diff, the failure cases, and the release decision. It works whether the assistant supplied three lines or a complete feature.

Write the contract before reviewing the solution

Describe the behavior in terms a reviewer can verify. For an endpoint that updates a saved collection, specify who may update it, which fields may change, what happens to unknown identifiers, and which response fields are public. Add a failure rule: if validation fails, no partial update should remain. This is a stronger review starting point than asking whether the implementation looks reasonable.

List the boundaries involved: browser to server, server to database, or server to an external service. Identify the sensitive data and permissions at each boundary. Keep production credentials, customer records, and unnecessary private context out of prompts and test fixtures. The reviewer needs representative inputs, not a copy of live user data.

Establish what actually changed

Inspect the patch before running unfamiliar code. In a Git repository, these read-only commands show the working tree and staged changes. They do not install dependencies or execute the proposed application.

git status --short
git diff --stat
git diff --check
git diff -- .
git diff --cached -- .

The ordinary diff excludes untracked files and staged edits; the staged diff covers the latter. Use the status output to identify new files and open them explicitly. The whitespace check is a formatting aid, not a correctness or security test. Compare the changed paths with the requested scope, including configuration, database migrations, lockfiles, and automation files.

For an existing review branch, use the team's agreed base rather than assuming the working-tree diff represents the whole proposal. Large unrelated refactors make a behavioral change harder to assess. Request a smaller patch when the reviewer cannot explain why each affected area belongs in the change.

Trace one input through the whole implementation

Start with a concrete request and follow its values through parsing, validation, authorization, storage, serialization, and logging. Find the actual library call behind each abstraction. Check official documentation for the installed version when an API or option is unfamiliar. A plausible method name is not evidence that the dependency supports it.

GitHub's responsible-use documentation for Copilot Chat describes limitations of generated output. Its Copilot Agents application card also addresses review limitations, including missed problems and false positives. Use machine feedback as a list of hypotheses to investigate. A second model agreeing with the first does not establish the behavior of the program.

Check authorization separately from authentication

In the collection example, a valid session only identifies the caller. The update must also establish that this caller may modify this particular collection. Review where that decision happens and whether every route to the write passes through it. Include background jobs or alternate endpoints if they invoke the same operation.

OWASP's authorization guidance supports reviewing access checks as explicit application behavior. Create two synthetic users and one collection owned by the first. Verify that the second cannot read restricted fields, update the collection, or infer private information through a different response path. Choose denial responses according to the application's documented policy.

Keep data separate from executable structure

Inspect database access, shell execution, template output, and filesystem paths. They have different controls; an input validator cannot replace all of them. For database queries, OWASP's SQL injection prevention guide explains parameter binding. Check that values are bound through the database interface rather than interpolated into a query string.

If a feature permits sorting, parameters usually cannot stand in for a column identifier. Map accepted sort keys to fixed application-owned query choices. A parameterized query also does not grant permission to access its returned row. These are separate review questions, and both need an answer.

Design tests that can disagree with the assistant

Derive cases from the contract rather than copying the implementation's branches into assertions. For the collection endpoint, test an allowed update, another user's request, a missing identifier, an oversized field, an unexpected property, and a storage failure. Assert the resulting stored state and public response, not merely a successful status code.

Where practical, run the new regression case against the earlier implementation to show that it detects the intended defect. If it passes both versions, inspect whether the test actually reaches the relevant behavior. This check is useful for a bug fix, but it is not meaningful to demand an earlier failure for every new feature.

Use the repository's documented test and analysis commands in an isolated environment with synthetic data. Read install hooks and unfamiliar scripts before executing them. A formatter passing proves little about permissions; a scanner finding no issue does not prove the absence of vulnerabilities. Combine focused automated checks with manual reasoning about the application contract.

Scale the review to the consequence of failure

A wording change and a payment calculation do not need the same evidence. Authorization, billing, destructive operations, migrations, and credential handling deserve deeper review and, where available, a second qualified reviewer. For a small helper, focused examples and the existing suite may be sufficient. Explain the choice in terms of consequences and uncertainty.

OWASP's secure code review guidance is a useful reference for structuring that inspection. Read context around the modified lines: a locally safe function can still receive untrusted data through another caller or expose a sensitive result through serialization. Review effort should follow those boundaries, not the apparent confidence of the generated explanation.

Make acceptance a recorded human decision

  • State the behavior accepted and the changed areas reviewed.
  • Record which checks ran, their results, and any unavailable environment.
  • Confirm permissions, failure handling, and response-field boundaries.
  • Document new dependencies and unresolved assumptions.
  • Identify the release owner, rollback approach, and signals requiring investigation.

After a revision, inspect the new diff and rerun checks affected by it. Do not carry forward an approval when the implementation has changed materially. If nobody can explain a sensitive branch, request a simpler implementation or obtain the missing expertise. The completion criterion is an understandable change supported by relevant evidence, with a human owner willing to accept the remaining uncertainty.
excerpt: Review AI-generated code against an explicit contract, trace permissions and data boundaries, design independent tests, and document the human acceptance decision.
seoTitle: A Human Workflow for Checking AI-Generated Code
seoDescription: Review AI-generated code with a human workflow for diffs, authorization, data boundaries, independent tests, risk-based checks, and recorded acceptance.
